en: Preface: Originally, principle is rooted in nature (*xing*); nature must have a path through which it is received. Form is partitioned by destiny (*ming*); destiny must have a treasury where it is gathered and fashioned.
The female of the True One (*zhen-yi*) grasps the basket and conceals the neck; how profoundly deep and pervasive this is! Therefore, the sagely spirit...
It is said that the Way is profound; it pursues the non-existence of sound and scent. The Awakened Virtue opens the source, reaching back to the silence where form and emptiness are severed.

From existence one enters non-existence, and from non-existence one enters further non-existence. Non-existence is like the myriad phenomena arising from the Great Ultimate (*taiji*), and the Great Ultimate arising from the Ultimateless (*wuji*).

Whether fundamental or derivative, subtle or coarse, principle and its traces coexist. As one follows the model and returns to transformation, the seasonal rhythms likewise follow suit. Thus it was in the past.
The ancients elucidated this with great precision. To enter into non-being while being unable to emerge from being is not the subtle art of shedding the tip of the blade.

If one cannot establish the ultimate standard (*ji*) despite its being infinite, this is not the function of concentrated solitude. Therefore, one who embodies the non-being (*wu*) values penetrating to that which is "not non-being" within non-being;
and one who takes the ultimate as their principle (*zongji*) circulates through the ultimate of every single thing.

When one reaches the ultimate of each and every thing, then the "one middle" is not a fixed center, yet it is the center at all times. The harmony already manifested is precisely the centrality prior to manifestation; thus, essence and function are one.

It penetrates all. There is neither non-existence nor existence; thus, one does not cling to emptiness as being non-empty, yet the characteristics of form return to emptiness. The characteristic of non-arising is itself the emptiness of non-extinction;
thus, the faculties and their objects are non-dual. The Great Way proceeds from a single source, and the profound and the long likewise follow the same track.
Alas, since the pure wind has long since vanished and the turbid atmosphere has grown ever more thick, the establishment of standards has caused the Truth to decline.

Those who divide the banks [of the Way] gallop after shadows, boasting of their mastery within the confines of the fences. These scholars of "owl-like" cunning enter the chamber only to brandish spears;
these men of drifting evasion embrace rocks while peddling jade. Consequently, true words are stalled by competitive disputation, and the fundamental truths become entangled with eccentric trappings.
Right and wrong are confused, names and reality are at odds and usurped. Counterfeit gems fill the space before us, while the refined essence is increasingly exhausted. Not so.
Alas, it is only that the transmission of the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius has been lost, and the true lineage of Kāśyapa Muni is likewise rare.

Sigh! To use water to extinguish water, or fire to extinguish fire—destiny becomes ever more complex; who can settle such matters? For the mind is neither defiled nor pure, just as water is neither clear nor turbid.
When a pearl is submerged in it, the water becomes clear; when an elephant enters it, the water becomes turbid. Though clarity and turbidity are one and the same water, they cannot be [confused].
To say that outside the water there is neither the image nor the pearl means that that which clarifies or disturbs it is precisely the mind. It is not the mind;

it is not not the mind—it is precisely the mind. This is why this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is so persistent and earnest in its instruction on subduing the mind through non-abiding, serving as the source of all dharmas. However, one must guard the Dharma without becoming attached to it.

If there is no method, then fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) remains incomplete; since awakening is obscured by consciousness, one must again return to the "abandonment of dharmas" (*śūnyatā-dharma*).
However, if one abandons dharmas without first practicing cultivation, the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) will not be established, and the fruit (*phala*) will likewise be difficult to achieve.

Therefore, the medicine of "annihilation" (*uccheda*) is prescribed. Now, as for annihilation: it is to cling to emptiness as being empty, seeing only emptiness while failing to see dharmas; thus, emptiness itself becomes a burden.

Regarding the Dharma: that which is not subject to cessation or extinction is empty according to how it is perceived. One uses emptiness to treat these perceptions; thus, perception itself becomes perfect emptiness.

Therefore, one skillfully relinquishes what is attained through relinquishment. Relinquishment serves as the bridge for reaching the shore; yet, to rely on relinquishment while seeking further relinquishment is like a stone falling into the depths.
Skillfully emptying [the mind] results in perfected vision; this vision is like a bright mirror being polished, whereas extinguishing vision constitutes emptiness.
Emptiness is like seeking illumination in a dark room; therefore it is said: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are like dreams, illusions, lamps, or cataracts.
This is because one returns from the conditioned to emptiness, rather than extinguishing the conditioned to achieve a semblance of emptiness.

In the profound resonance of the Sage, the two principles are intertwined and the cloud-like script is brilliantly manifest, as clear as a row of eyebrows. It is not as those in the world claim, who merely say that non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) is already [the goal].

It is merely hearing the mark of emptiness. Thus, those whose true mind turns toward study yet lose it take quiescent extinction to be emptiness and the realization of solitude to be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
These are called those who turn their minds toward study yet lose it; they take non-extinction to be emptiness and heedless indulgence to be the unconditioned.
This extends even to those at the rivers and lakes or in the declining days [of the age], who become bound by legalism and profit, and harbor power, intrigue, and arrogance.

Those engaged in the poultry and beast-taming trades, those who indulge in poison, and those who live in squalor, gluttony, and lust—there is none among them who cannot designate themselves by the title of Bodhisattva. Alas!
The reason the Buddha delivers sentient beings is to deliver them from the gateway of birth and death. He causes the mind to descend so as to purify its defilements;
he employs non-abiding to refine one's progress; he uses giving to perfect one’s merit; and he employs the mark of emptiness to investigate his [the Buddha’s]...
Fourth is the "incomparable elevation. If one is able to purify and advance, yet does not contemplate the ultimate goal, one will abandon the path midway.
If one seeks only the ultimate without necessarily applying diligent effort, it is like failing to examine the root while attempting to align the tip.
To delight in giving and delight in saving others, yet fail to realize the ultimate meaning for oneself—this is the inferior grade of *dāna*.

To be able to realize the ultimate meaning for oneself, yet be unable to benefit others or awaken them, is not the unsurpassed *bodhi*. The plum ripens in its own time; when the wind ceases, the water naturally settles.

To remedy these shortcomings, nothing is better than to focus exclusively on the unity of understanding and practice (*vidyā-caryā*). When understanding and practice reach their profound depths, one will ultimately achieve perfect self-realization. I—
By nature I am dull-witted and incapable of deep understanding. Nevertheless, how could I not be struck with awe by the fears of the Final Dharma?
Having happened to recite the True Sūtras, I have, quite spontaneously, produced many words—merely a collection of snares and traps.

Since I cannot transcend what is seen beyond language and characters, I have nonetheless added my own superfluous chatter amidst the explanations of the chapters and verses. For to discourse upon the essence while severing all principle...
How could I dare? If one may derive meaning from the text, there might be something to be gained. Even among a thousand deliberations of the ignorant, there must be one instance of attainment;

even the words of a commoner gathering grass and firewood are what the sages select. Thus, perhaps my labor, which is but a single scoop from the ocean, or my contribution, which is but a single hair upon the ground, will be pardoned by the Awakened King.
However, compared to previous commentaries, my own fabrications are indeed many. I am aware...
My own faults and those of others must necessarily be shared equally; therefore, I dare not rely upon the prestige of my title, nor do I dare borrow the luster of your great reputation.
I truly fear that one who is merely "a jade-crowned reed" might bring reproach upon your noble lineage.
Thus, I have briefly set forth my own observations as they are, awaiting the definitive judgment of the wise eyes of the ten directions.
Xu Fa of Nanhu Garden examines the discrepancies:
According to the Golden Sūtra, there are five translations; yet those recited in the world today are the Qin translation. However, recent versions mostly differ from the ancient ones.
The original versions were not the same; they have undergone various additions and alterations over time. From my humble perspective, none are as exquisite as the ancient texts.
Moreover, regarding sacred traces and the true source, how can they be subject to alteration?

I have heard an elderly monk say that for those who recite the Golden Sutra, the merit is most supernatural, yet if even a single character is mistaken, there will be no efficacy. One must be cautious! Now, all [versions] follow Zhao Ziaoyang.
The stone carving records this; it differs from recent editions. Furthermore, all the various scholarly collations and commentaries are preserved here.
Regarding the second section, it should read "How should one dwell? (云何應住); the current edition reads "How should one abide? (云何應住). Even retaining the character "abide" (住) is already incorrect.

Regarding the term "real mark" (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), the character "should" (*yīng*) should not be added. However, in the original translations from the Qin and Zhou periods, both read "should abide" (*yīng zhù*).
Only the Wei translation reads "should say how to abide" (*yīng yún hé zhù*); thus, the Zhao edition is likewise not without its textual basis.
13. In the current edition, there are perhaps seven characters—namely "is named Prajñāpāramitā"—that are missing; however, they are present in the Zhao carving.

Nevertheless, these seven characters are truly absent from the original translation. Although the Zhao version is closer to reason and has been followed by many in recent times, we have nonetheless retained them here.

Section Fourteen. One should give rise to resentment; in the current edition, it is sometimes written as "wrathful eyes," but according to the collated translations and the Zhao carving, both read "resentment.
Regarding the passage "The Perfection of Forbearance taught by the Tathāgata is not the Perfection of Forbearance," the current edition further...
There are these seven characters, "This is called the Perfection of Forbearance" (忍辱波羅蜜). Both the earlier translation and the Zhao edition lack them.
Examining the phrase for the first *pāramitā*, it concludes the preceding discourse and thus its meaning is complete.
The phrase for the Perfection of Forbearance initiates the subsequent discourse and is therefore incomplete; it should not be added. Now, I follow the Zhao edition.
Regarding the phrase "for the benefit of all sentient beings," the current edition contains an extra character "gu" (hence), which is absent in both the Huìyì and Zhào editions;
it has now been deleted. Section Seventeen.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."

Regarding the phrase "those who have generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*": the current edition lacks the character "ruò" (若). However, both the Zhao edition and Zongle’s annotated version, produced by imperial decree, include it.
Since this refers to those currently present [in the assembly], the inclusion of the character "ruò" is appropriate; its syntactic force is very lively, and one should follow these editions.

Twenty-four parts [of the former] do not equal even one part [of the latter]. Furthermore, the current edition contains an additional hundred characters, or perhaps one extra character for every thousand characters.
These were absent from both the Wei translation and the Zhao carving; as the punctuation is unclear, it hinders comprehension.
Twenty-sixth section. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses. In the translations from the Zhou and Wei dynasties, all instances read "yan" (words).
The current edition reads "jie" (verses), which has been altered by secular scribes; following the Zhao edition, they are rendered as "yan."
Thirty minutes. Would this multitude of atoms be considered many? (Note: The current edition adds the four characters "Subhūti said," which are absent in both the Huìyì and Zhào editions.)
If one considers the entire scripture, the character "則" (zé) has been changed to "即" (jí) in many instances in the current edition—more than twenty such cases can be observed.
Although the two meanings of "則" and "即" are not significantly different, there is a subtle distinction in their tonal nuance: "即" is a term denoting that something has already occurred.
This is, therefore, a term referring to what has not yet occurred. For instance, "the Wheel-Turning Sage King is the Tathāgata" is a very flexible expression;

were it changed to the word "is already" (即), it would become rigid and lifeless. This is why there arises the erroneous interpretation that the Wheel-Turning King is actually identical to the Tathāgata.
Otherwise, if one takes these as signs with the mind, one becomes attached to self, person, sentient beings, and a life-span.
For instance, if it were the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he would not have bestowed the prediction upon me;
if there were a Buddha existing in reality, he would not have spoken of this multitude of atoms. All instances of the character "則" (zé) must be excised and cannot be altered.

Although other characters may admit of two interpretations based on their meaning, the distinction between the elegant (classical) and the vernacular is self-evident; all shall be corrected according to the Zhao edition based on the three translations.

Examining the various translations, there are many significant differences. Only the Qin translation is the most concise; it appeared earliest, while subsequent versions gradually became more extensive and detailed.
This is because the founder finds it difficult to exert effort, whereas those who follow find it easier to achieve refinement—a principle that is naturally so.
Yet, as for adding embellishments and seeking beauty, it is not as good as returning to simplicity and rusticity to capture the truth. Therefore...
It is not without reason that the *Shi ben* (Origins of the World) alone honors the Qin translation. Now, although I have examined variant texts, I cannot describe them all in detail.
Only the Wei translation of the twelve divisions of the canon is relatively concise and essential, sufficient for the elucidation of its chapters and sentences;
it is therefore appended here for reference.
Thus have I heard... up to "having spread out his seat, he sat down. This constitutes the first section, the Prologue.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti... up to "well-entrusted to all bodhisattvas. This constitutes the second section, the Entrustment through Protective Recollection.
"World-Honored One, son of good family, I am most desirous to hear [this]. This is the third section, 'Abiding in the Divisions.
The Buddha told Subhūti: 'One should simply abide as instructed. This is the fourth section, 'Practice According to Reality.'"
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? This is the fifth section, titled "Whether the Tathāgata Exists or Does Not Exist as Unconditioned.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "All worthy sages and saints exist by means of the unconditioned dharma."
The Distinction. This constitutes the sixth section on the emptiness of self and phenomena.
Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the trichiliocosm [with merit], this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.
This constitutes the seventh section on the comparison of fully accomplished merits.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells with the mind attached to phenomena while practicing giving, how much more so when they write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and explain it to others? This concludes the eighth section on Suchness (*tathatā*).
Subhūti, to speak in brief: even the resulting retribution is inconceivable. This concludes the ninth section, "On Benefiting Others.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha: [this continues] up to "the immovability of suchness. This concludes the tenth section, "On Severing Doubts."
Tenth: The eleventh section, "The Four-Line Verse as the Non-Abiding Path. Eleventh:
Following the Buddha’s preaching of this sutra, the twelfth section, "Circulation."
Regarding these twelve sections, compared to Dao’an’s version they are more detailed, while compared to the *Zhao ming* [edition] they are more concise;
they capture the essential framework quite well. Furthermore, from Subhūti’s repeated questioning onwards, all serve to resolve doubts, which is particularly a correct insight.
Moreover, in the seventeenth section, Subhūti again asks: "How should a son or daughter of good family who has set forth toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
Regarding the phrase "the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," the Wei translation states at the beginning:
"How does a bodhisattva, within the Mahāyāna, give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? whereas at the end it simply says:
"How does a bodhisattva give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"—thus omitting the term "Mahāyāna."
The three characters in the middle clearly possess two meanings: a shallow and a profound. That which is called the "Mahāyāna" is precisely the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The fact that the subsequent question does not mention the Mahāyāna indicates that it refers specifically to the practice of the bodhisattva path in the present.
This passage is sufficient as one piece of evidence for the causal conditions of the three periods of time. Regarding this, after my draft was completed...
Later, upon reading this edition, I felt somewhat fortunate that it did not greatly deviate from the ancients. This led me to recall the words of Master Yuan Liaofan:
"If there are points in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that you do not understand, simply read the various translations and you will see [the meaning] for yourself.
This was all the more convincing to me.
Furthermore, Paramārtha’s translation states: "Unmoving as suchness (tathatā), there is always the correct teaching.
One should contemplate conditioned phenomena as being like darkness, cataracts, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud.

Regarding what is called "always the correct teaching," it means that within the constant discourse, there is the established teaching. I maintain that these final four lines represent the ancient tradition.
Verse: This is also one piece of evidence. Once the book was completed, my elder brother Qian Dengming showed me three translated versions, and only then was I able to see them.
Furthermore, Master Zhongfeng’s *Brief Commentary* states: "The Tathāgata preached the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in six hundred fascicles during the fourth period;

the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* is but one of them. Regarding these six hundred [fascicles], commentators [have said]: [...]* *I have provided the structural context of the fragmentary text based on the provided source.*
The general outline of this volume is subsumed under the four characters "Fusion," "Penetration," "Refinement," and "Elimination.

This is because, in the second period, the Tathāgata turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park to certify the various Hīnayāna practitioners, leading them to enter the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Since this did not accord with his original intention, he subsequently employed Vimalakīrti in the third period to critique and refute them, thereby...

First, one feels shame for the small and aspires toward the great. Thereafter, one extensively explains the single flavor of *prajñā* and true emptiness specifically for those of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), thereby dissolving their attachments and unblocking their obstructions. One washes and purifies them, like cleansing a defiled vessel until it is clean and pure;
only then does one pour upon them the nectar-flavor of the perfect and sudden Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). This is merely gold.
The Diamond Sūtra is constrained by its concise phrasing; it is nearly impossible to parse its sentences and read it aloud.
Its meaning is profound and is entrusted within these six hundred fascicles. If there are passages therein that you cannot fully comprehend, you need not harbor doubts.
Simply maintain a single thought of deep faith, and after a time, you will understand them naturally. This is what is meant by "the single flavor of true emptiness," which is exclusively for—
The followers of the Hīnayāna dissolve their attachments and penetrate their obstructions; these words are sufficient to encompass the entire treasury of the Golden Sūtra.

This is because the followers of the Hīnayāna differ from those who have newly begun their study of the Buddha’s teachings: their practice and realization are already profound, yet they have simply not yet entered the Mahāyāna.
They are precisely what is called "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Therefore, it is said: "All conditioned phenomena..."
Regarding the Dharma, one should contemplate it in this manner. This treatise is particularly sufficient for elucidating the four-line verse.
I reflect that in the past, when Master Zhao Wuxing served Master Zhongfeng, he transcribed this sutra by hand and presented it to his master for perusal;
this is the very stone carving we have today. It is certain that the characters and phrases within were scrutinized by two great eyes, ensuring there are no errors whatsoever. Thus, I—
In examining the variations [of the text], I have corrected them all in accordance with the Shí edition; this is sufficient as a standard.

Furthermore, regarding the sixth section, following the passage "There is no mark of phenomena, nor is there any mark of non-phenomena," the *Jíjiě* (Collected Explanations) states that the old edition additionally contained the phrase "no mark, nor is it not without mark. Therefore, Maitreya’s verse says: "Based on the eightfold eightfold meaning..."
Now, according to the translation by Bodhiruci: "There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there no mark of dharmas;

there is no mark, nor is there no non-mark. According to the translation by Paramārtha: "There is no perception of dharmas, nor perception of non-dharmas; there is no perception, nor perception of non-perception."
Since all translations follow the same track, the old edition is indeed authentic. Nevertheless, even the Zhao edition lacks this;

as it has been handed down for so long, I did not dare to add it arbitrarily. However, upon carefully savoring the final eight lines, I find that they encompass both aspects—like the Buddha’s dual reception—and that these two meanings truly exist.
Specifically, when speaking from the perspective of past Tathāgatas, one speaks of "marks" (xiàng); when speaking from the perspective of the present Buddha...
As for the words, they are called "Dharma," yet while their principle is uniform, their textual expressions lead to different inclinations.
Therefore, I have distinguished them within these chapters and sentences; indeed, these two phrases are the essential points for grasping the main framework.
Generally speaking, the Buddha’s words necessarily present the whole body [of the teaching], lest virtue easily fall into partial views; thus, I have deleted them. This...
This is precisely what Zhongfeng meant by that which "cannot be explained through a single interpretation.

For example, Confucius emphasized only benevolence (*ren*), whereas Mencius also brought forth righteousness (*yi*) alongside it. While speaking of benevolence alone, righteousness is naturally contained within it;
yet when righteousness is brought forth alongside it, benevolence may seem as though it is not the complete virtue. This is where the stages of the sages and worthies differ.

Later students must personally investigate the ultimate root and foundation; they must not merely consume the teacher’s words like food heard through the ears and then simply copy them like drawing a gourd from a model.
Furthermore, regarding the thirty-two sections: if there are good men or good women who give rise to the bodhicitta, [the Bodhisattva]...
[The character] "sa" (薩). In many secular editions, this is frequently erroneously written as "ti" (提).
According to the original manuscript of the *Huìyì* (會譯), the stone-carved edition of Zhao [Mengfu], Zongle’s edition with Imperial Edict Commentary, and Yunqi’s *Bǐlùn* (鎞論), all read "sa.
This phrase precisely concludes the seventeenth section, concerning Subhūti as a good man or good woman present at the assembly in the Jeta Grove.

Questioning the intent of the Bodhisattva’s practice: regarding the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), it has already been stated that "the Bodhisattva is likewise so," and further that "one who penetrates the dharma of non-self is called a true Bodhisattva.
Regarding merit, it is said that "this Bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former Bodhisattva. Reaching this point of culmination, it is further stated:
If good sons or good daughters give rise to the bodhisattva mind, their preceding and succeeding elements will correspond to one another, with a continuity like a thread.
If they were to change this to "bodhi," it would become diffuse and disordered. This is why the principles of this chapter must be understood clearly.
A Brief General Discourse (Ten Points):
The Buddha-dharma has two gates, the doctrinal and the sectarian. To reach its ultimate conclusion, they originally belong to a single convergence.

This is like the Confucian distinction between those who know by birth and those who know through learning; both ultimately converge in the state of sagehood. Now, the Sectarian Gate speaks only of sudden enlightenment, regardless of whether [gradual cultivation] is required.

[Note: The sutras and treatises are also quite verbose. I reflect that the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states that the wondrous clarity of essential awareness is neither caused nor conditioned, nor is it spontaneous.
If this is so, then not only would there be no need to establish the Teachings (*śāsana*), but how could there even be a School (*zong*)?
Yet, when Śākyamuni ascended the seat and Mañjuśrī raised his staff, five hundred non-Buddhists fled upon seeing its shadow. Why, then, is there still [this proliferation]?

The various teachings amount to more than three thousand five hundred fascicles. This is because while the Buddha-nature is possessed by every person, there are ten thousand differences between those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In principle, there is sudden enlightenment; in practice, there is no sudden elimination.

Therefore, following the section on the realization of the Way (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is ultimately taught once again. It is just like the "Sincerity" chapter of the *Zhongyong*.

The luminous clarity of truth must not be neglected in either aspect; thus, there are the three trainings in the outflows-free state and the sequence of the four types of discipline to lead one forward.
In essence, although enlightened awareness is perfect, it does not achieve its fruition without verbal teaching;
the transformation by seasonal rain has its own proper timing. If one were to take an ordinary person on the road and name them "suddenly awakened," how could they ever reach the other shore?
How lamentable! Lately, the Zen school has been quite renowned for its great flourishing; yet, the teachings have ultimately remained unclarified.

This is truly because people seek shortcuts while loathing diligent effort. Upon investigation, such shortcuts never lead to the further shore, and those who loathe toil merely lose their own true nature.
Those of superior capacity spend half their lives in bewildered confusion, resulting entirely in demonic obstacles; those of inferior capacity merely follow after sensory dust.

Conversely, when one is bound by their own actions, the karma created becomes increasingly deep. Therefore, I have compiled this collection, striving for explanations that are coarse and shallow, merely to make it easy for beginners to understand, so that they may find the gate and gain access to the path;

once they can ascend into the hall and enter the inner chamber, and through the accumulation of practice their merit becomes profound, they will naturally be able to realize emptiness and attain thorough awakening.
This is not intended as a mere verbal substitute or to add legs to a snake; rather, it is meant to ensure that those who seek to transcend words do not fall into ruin.
Eighth, regarding the "Signless": If one is a great elephant among the wise, with a jewel within his robes, he certainly has no need for the illumination of a firefly.

There are no fewer than several hundred kinds of commentaries on the Golden Sūtra; now that the grand music of the celestial realm has been performed, why should one still require the vulgar songs of the common folk?
Nevertheless, there is something I cannot help but feel: I have observed that all previous commentaries have relied upon Chan...

The patriarchs investigated the dialogues, and the masters of old raised their meanings, compiling them into books. Furthermore, they clarified the thirty-two divisions [of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*], yet this obscured and obstructed the eye of wisdom.
Thus, there arose those who overturned the molds and swept away the furrows; however, these works remained fragmented, miscellaneous, and trivial.

They do not seek out the textual lineages, nor do they discern the sequence or the depth of meaning; thus, while their grasp of doctrine becomes increasingly broad, the intent of the sutras grows ever more obscure.
To cite doctrinal points as topics for discussion is akin to the Confucian practice of composing formal examination essays:

one seizes upon a given topic and offers a set of arguments, yet this is certainly not arriving at the destination. Without it, one cannot perceive the true countenance of the original text. It is like [the following] analogy:
To excerpt passages and compose lectures—who could possibly grasp the spirit of the text or its underlying breath?
By nature, I have always preferred reading the scriptures over commentaries; therefore, for this collection, I have focused exclusively on reciting the canonical text itself.

For several years, I have contemplated it deeply and attained silent realization, little realizing that within the scripture there exists a natural progression of stages and the causal conditions of dialogue, even in the case of the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing* (Lotus Sūtra).
Maitreya’s verses have also already pointed this out. However, traditional commentators have followed established conventions and directly grasped only the aspect of emptiness;

they have also frequently misinterpreted Maitreya’s verses. They fail to realize that this sutra originally proceeds from the discourse on the aspect of existence to the aspect of emptiness, using Subhūti’s doubt regarding the differing aspects of the three periods of time to explain the single dharma throughout the three periods.

It is signless (*animitta*). Because there is a distinction between the Tathāgata and the Buddha regarding past and present characteristics, after the seventeenth chapter, Śūnyatā-sambhava again asks about the Buddha-dharma, and the Buddha speaks of the non-existence of self and dharmas (*anātma-dharma*) to destroy that notion of difference.
Now, those who explain this fail to make any distinctions; consequently, the various doubts and the various analytical deconstructions that follow seem like redundant repetitions.
In the questions posed by the Tathāgata, there are four layers; in the examples comparing the superiority of merit, there are nine grades.
The clumsy repeatedly state their reasoning without realizing its prolixity, while the clever twist their intentions [to avoid it].

They engage in forced interpretations without realizing their errors; thus, a single exchange of questions and answers from Kāśyapa and Mahākāśyapa—its profound depths and historical origins—is entirely obscured.
This is like blocking the main entrance while boasting about the inner sanctum; how could this be true insight?
It is for this reason that I cannot restrain myself. For now, I shall briefly highlight one or two essential points to seek the correction of the True Dharma Eye.
This is discussed in other views. It is certainly not merely a fondness for novelty intended to expose the errors of predecessors;
rather, it is truly out of fear that complacency will compound the mistakes of future generations.

Regarding the term "Tathāgata," previous interpretations simply state that it means "true nature is as-it-is" (tathatā) or "coming according to principle" (tathā-āgata), without specifying which person it refers to.
This means that the Buddha is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Buddha. The purport of the sutra lies in the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
why must one differentiate and analyze? I maintain that this is the ultimate reality.

If one were to provide an exegesis and explanation, then "Tathāgata" is originally the name for Śākyamuni Buddha’s *dharmakāya* during his stage of practice (*bhūmi*), which is a past manifestation. Therefore, throughout this entire sutra, Subhūti...
When he refers to the "Tathāgata," his intention actually points to the Buddha; yet the Buddha answers from the perspective of the causal stage.
Therefore, he repeatedly mentions what the Tathāgata has said, what the Tathāgata constantly says, and what the Tathāgata said after his parinirvāṇa:

"In the past, at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he was granted the prediction that he would attain Buddhahood. This is because Dīpaṃkara was also titled "Tathāgata. (From the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Mañjuśrī...)

What is called the "ground" (*bhūmi*) also refers to the past; this sutra merely abbreviates the phrasing.

This is why the Buddha first answers the question on subduing the mind, next answers the question on non-abiding, and subsequently answers the question on seeing the Tathāgata. With three questions and three answers, the beginning and end are perfectly complete.
The great sections of the Buddha’s Dharma truly conclude here; this is indeed the mind transmitted by the Tathāgatas through the ages.
Because it is the Dharma, the Buddha himself also refers to it as a *sūtra*.

From the fifth section (*pañcavarga*) onwards, following Subhūti’s inquiry regarding faithful acceptance and upholding, he further elaborates upon it, saying: "without grasping," "without speaking," and "without attainment."
It is said: "The foremost rarity," "the practice of patience and giving," and "the eradication of karmic offenses.
None of these transcend the meaning of subduing the mind through cultivation that is non-abiding and signless.
This which I call the Dharma of the Tathāgata truly refers to the Tathāgatas of the past. However, Subhūti originally addressed the Buddha as "Tathāgata," yet the Buddha did not...
One might ask: "How can one know that the Buddha and the Tathāgata do not possess distinct dharmas?
Thereupon, in the seventeenth section, [the text] again intimately addresses the various bodhisattvas present in the assembly at Jeta Grove, who inquire about the Dharma of the present Buddha.

Therefore, he uses the prophecy of Dīpaṃkara’s attainment of Buddhahood as proof. Furthermore, he elucidates this through the fact that the mind of the three periods of time is ungraspable.
Below, he again compares the Buddha and the Tathāgata side-by-side to inquire about them. Thus, having reached this point, the Buddha—
At the outset, [the Buddha] sets forth the matter with full clarity, identifying himself as the Tathāgata;
and Subhūti likewise understands that the Buddha is indeed the Tathāgata, for there is no duality between them throughout the three periods of time.

Thereupon, he further poses a question on behalf of future sentient beings, whereby the single Dharma of the three periods of time is revealed in its brilliant completeness. Finally, in each successive section, he treats the Buddha and the Tathāgata [as one].
Examining the three periods of time together to their ultimate depth, they all return to the single dharma of formlessness (*animitta*).

This is the true countenance of the causes and conditions of the questions and answers in this assembly at Jeta’s Grove. One must speak from the perspective of diverse characteristics (*nānātva-lakṣaṇa*) to reach the single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*);
therefore it is said: "neither identical nor different. By speaking from the three periods of time to reach the single dharma, it is said: "Thus knowing, thus seeing, thus [understanding]."

Faithful understanding does not give rise to the marks of dharmas; this is precisely what is meant by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. Nowadays, various schools are muddled together, so it is necessary to distinguish them.
The "four-line verse" refers to the four lines concerning all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Indeed, this verse has been transmitted since antiquity.
The verse of this transmission is something people have long heard and long known; therefore, it is presented here at the very end. Its meaning truly encompasses the entire body of the Buddha-dharma.
Later generations have misinterpreted the three characters "yǒuwéifǎ" (conditioned phenomena), characterizing them merely through the single term "emptiness."

As for these roots of goodness, it is because they have not attained the Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā that they fall into error: by entering the gate of Abhidharma, they fall into the extreme of existence;

by entering the gate of emptiness, they fall into the extreme of non-existence; and by entering the gate of Saṃyukta-ābhidharma-hṛdaya (Kuṇḍala), they fall into the extreme of both existence and non-existence.
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "It is not because there are no persons that it is called 'empty'; rather, phenomena are empty by their very nature.
It is not that form is empty because it has been extinguished. If one attains emptiness and yet relies upon emptiness, the Buddha says that such a person is falling into decline.
Noble son, it would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to overweening pride based on a view of emptiness."
Why is this? All views are liberated through emptiness; however, if one gives rise to a view of emptiness, it cannot be cured.
Therefore, the "Pervasion of the Fundamental Tenet" asks: "How should one abide? As for what is meant by "abiding," it is not like the abiding of ordinary beings in signs.
Furthermore, it is not like the practitioners of the Two Vehicles who dwell in emptiness; rather, one dwells in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is neither provisional nor empty; it is the Truth of the Middle Way. How does one subdue the mind?

What is called "subduing" is not like the practice of ordinary beings, who suppress the six consciousnesses, nor is it like the practice of the Two Vehicles, who annihilate the seventh consciousness. Rather, it is...
The subtle habitual tendencies within the field of the eight consciousnesses are perfumed by True Suchness (*tathatā*), causing the evolving consciousnesses to be transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*).
This is like subduing a band of rebels and turning them into law-abiding citizens; this is precisely what is meant by "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Indeed, the Buddha-dharma is truly not something realized through mere emptiness. Therefore, throughout the entire sutra, the discourse proceeds from the existence of phenomena to the signlessness of phenomena. At the very end, furthermore—
To speak clearly and explicitly, one does not produce the mark of annihilation. Therefore, six matters are used as analogies;
in all six matters, there is a transition from existence to non-existence. Likewise, the Buddha-dharma proceeds from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus it is said: "All conditioned phenomena. This refers to what is taught in the sūtras: subduing the mind, non-abiding, faith, upholding, the most rare, and patience (*kṣānti*).
Do not begrudge giving; you should give rise to the mind without dwelling upon it. Accomplish patience and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, without forming the mark of annihilation.
To uphold this sutra and expound it for others—all these are what are called conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Yet all of these ultimately reach the state where there are no marks of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore it is said: "One should contemplate in this manner.

This is precisely what is called *nirvāṇa without remainder*; it is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Now, some commentators have erroneously taken the three characters "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) to mean the flux and creative activity within the realm of sentient beings. In the center, one attains stainless sovereignty. Clearly and explicitly, the character "mid" (zhōng) is pointed out; it is the character for "attaining.
If one abandons the Dharma to seek emptiness, that is but a dull emptiness, not true emptiness. How could this be the correct meaning of this verse?
Having read this entire Golden Sutra, its thousands of words and myriad phrases all culminate in this verse and this meaning. Therefore, why is this so?
The following sentence connects [the previous thought]: it clarifies that this is a codification based on the ancestral tradition and transmits the essential secret instructions.

Now, there are those who claim there are twenty-six divisions of four lines each; however, they fail to realize that the "twenty-six divisions" refers to the fact that in the preceding text, where it says, "At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses," and so forth, it can be understood that these were chanted all at once during the intervals between the World-Honored One’s questions and answers. Why?
If one can anticipate and explain [the meaning] beforehand, how much more so after the twenty-sixth section? Why then should one not be able to recite and expound it alone?

Furthermore, regarding those who speak of the four phrases concerning the mark of self (*ātman*) and the mark of person (*pudgala*), they do not realize that the original structure of the verses consists of four types:
first, *anuṣṭubh*; second, *gāthā*; third, *geya*; and fourth, *udāna*. At the beginning, all...
Thirty-two characters constitute one *gāthā*. This is essentially the ancient style of four-character lines in eight sentences.
Later, these gradually evolved into either five-character or seven-character lines; thus, the *gāthā* possesses its own distinct metrical form.
If any four-line structure were considered a *gāthā*, then what could not be made into a *gāthā*? Why then do we restrict the term to only four lines? There are even those who, using the *Vajra*...
Regarding the division of the eight characters of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* into four lines:

there are those who designate a verse (*gāthā*) when the meaning is fully expressed through four lines; furthermore, there are those who refer to one line, two lines, three lines, or even four lines [as a verse].

As for those who offer hundreds of thousands of interpretations, they merely engage in further forced exegesis; in the end, they fail to realize that the radiance of the Muni’s jewel is spontaneously manifesting in the sky, and no one is willing to believe it.
The past mind is unattainable; the present mind is unattainable; the future mind is unattainable. These three phrases constitute the pivotal key to the entire sutra.

Because Subhūti raised his question again based on the existence of conceptual characteristics (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*), [the Buddha] refuted this by showing that the minds of the three periods of time are all unattainable.
Therefore, he proceeded to enumerate the five eyes, explaining them layer by layer, with the essential aim of...
To know the various minds of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the three periods of time is exceedingly difficult; yet the Buddha knows them all, and for this reason it is marvelous.
If one were to explain it now, one might say that within a single day or a single moment, these three kinds of mind exist. This is corroborated by citing the *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya-sūtra*.
However, those who do not know the *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya-sūtra* fail to understand how the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī brings about deliverance.
For those who have committed acts of killing, it is essential to see the meaning of attaining Buddhahood swiftly by turning one's head for even a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*).
Therefore, within the span of a single moment, the past, present, and future are distinguished in order to inspire faith in people.

If this sutra follows the Buddhist Dharma from above regarding non-self (*anātman*), how does it relate to the three minds within a single moment? If there are three minds within a single moment, why is that necessarily so?
To speak with such gravity, one must look as far back as the sentient beings of the five eyes’ world;

how much more so, then, regarding the original text of the *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya*, which states that [the Buddha] cannot be apprehended across the three periods of time, and thus has never been restricted to a single moment.

As for the "adornment of Buddha-lands," this refers to whether the various Bodhisattvas, while in the assembly within the Tathāgata’s Buddha-land, conceive of such adornments or whether they actually construct palaces, halls, and other such forms.
To claim that their bodies are like Sumeru, the king of mountains, is a metaphorical statement from which no literal meaning can be derived;
therefore, the preceding text specifically adds the two characters "譬若" (pìruò—like as if) to clarify that it is not so.
Regarding "true words" (*satyavāda*): some take this to mean that the golden body was truly three *zhang* in height.

If one respects a disciple, it is simply like saying, "as the disciple reveres the Buddha," which is an inverted construction; there are many such examples in the Buddhist scriptures, what is called the "reversal of the teaching.
Such is the idiomatic usage in the West (India); for instance, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is not [to be taken literally as] "No, World-Honored One."
"Venerable One," both instances are inverted constructions. For example, regarding the phrases "What do you think? and "For what reason," etc., they are all presented in reverse order.
This is the actual principle throughout the entire sutra; therefore, even the four-line verse is placed at the very end. Such is the natural flow of the language;
thus, both the grammatical structure and the structural logic of the text are like this. It may be that some take it to mean: "If [the Buddha] were so venerable..."

The elder brother Manjushri and the elder brother Samantabhadra did not realize that their own reverence for their younger brothers was ultimately not equal to the reverence shown by those younger brothers toward their teachers.
How could such profound sutras, which are like the stupas and temples of the Buddha, be treated as merely equivalent to the reverence a teacher shows toward his disciples?
The question regarding the physical marks (lakṣaṇa) was raised four times; it is the division of the body according to the vision of reality as it is.
"Characteristics" refers to the characteristics of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). This is an investigation based on the coarse traces of the past and present, proceeding from the shallow to the deep;
hence it is said: "All that has characteristics is entirely illusory. This is precisely the wondrous function of the Buddha’s capacity to lead one to awakening by means of the objective realm.

Regarding the "receiving and upholding according to the Dharma," this is divided into the thirty-two marks; these are the characteristics of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The Dharma-body is not something heard with the ears.
Within the range of vision, the world is neither world nor non-world, and atoms are neither atoms nor non-atoms.

Because one perceives the Dharma-body as being neither true form nor non-form, this is already one level deeper than merely comparing the physical body to non-form. This reaches the stage of "departing from form and departing from characteristics."
To inquire of the Buddha by means of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and to inquire of the Tathāgata by means of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), both are incomplete, yet both are called complete.
Thus, what is seen is not seeing, yet that which is not seeing may also be called seeing; such a principle is perfect and more profound than the former.
If the dharma-body is not a portion of form, can one contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? Contemplate.
This differs from the previous views. In those [previous] views, the observer was "there" while the contemplation was "here"; the observer was "outside" while the contemplation was "inside.

In meaning, this comparison is the most subtle and profound among the three preceding questions. Therefore, Subhūti said, "So it is, so it is," yet even here, the place where false conceptualization has not been purified remains.

The Buddha then awakened him by means of the analogy of the Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin). Regarding the four statements concerning the physical marks (lakṣaṇa) that precede and follow, there are differences in their depth and shallowness.
The levels [of meaning] clearly differ, yet commentators treat them all as uniform abstruse talk, remaining utterly without discrimination.
Consequently, when Subhūti responds to the question of how one should contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, they forcibly insert the word "not" (*na*).

Thus, they alter the words "just so, just so" (*evam eva*) into the Buddha’s own speech, and their commentary claims this is a misplaced passage (*vyatyasta-pāṭha*). They further assert that a universal monarch (*cakravartin-rāja*) is, therefore, the Tathāgata.
The character "改" (gǎi) is changed to "即" (jí). It is asserted that the Wheel-Turning King and the Tathāgata are of one and the same appearance.

Furthermore, the question "Can the Buddha be seen by means of a body endowed with [physical] form? is assigned to the eighty minor marks (aśīty-anuvyañjana), while "Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of a body endowed with all the [major] marks?
is assigned to the thirty-two major marks (dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa); both are mere fabrications. This is entirely due to [the confusion between] "Buddha" and "Tathāgata. Regarding the three...
Regarding the causes and conditions of the world, they have never been clearly distinguished, leading to these conjectures.

Subsequent generations have followed and perpetuated these errors until they became deeply rooted and incurable, thereby forever obscuring the True Dharma of Kāśyapa. This is truly a matter for profound lamentation.
Therefore, I have not hesitated to correct each point accordingly. Those who understand me will be fellow Buddhists; those who condemn me will also be fellow Buddhists.

The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is.

previously, I examined it by way of its doctrinal meaning. Recently, having compiled a commentary on the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, I finally categorized it according to the sūtra texts and annotated it section by section, which may serve as a marvelous mirror for the moon [of the Dharma].
I was able to read this final portion, and I did not expect such an essential teaching for the three periods of time.
The meaning is perfectly clear and harmonious; yet, as for those who have spoken of it in the past, many remain obscure.
Not only do their commentaries on the scriptural text contain errors from beginning to end, but they offer even more divergent interpretations regarding the fundamental tenets of the Three Periods.

This is entirely due to being fettered by preconceived views, refusing to shift the boat to reach the shore, and instead stubbornly clinging to the notion that a raw jade stone is merely a mouse. Therefore, I have specifically marked these points for clarity.
I shall provide a brief commentary on these points. As stated in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra* regarding one's own person and the repayment of kindness:

"If one is not attached to the fruits of retribution, does not guard oneself by withholding gifts, and does not seek other matters, this is the correct explanation; one should simply abide as instructed."
The traditional interpretation shifts this to the explanation of "giving by not dwelling on form, and giving by not dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomena.

How does this relate to the meaning of karmic retribution? Within the context of subduing and training those [beings], it involves distancing oneself from the mind that grasps at signs (*nimitta*) and severing various doubts, while also preventing the arising of a productive [conceptual] mind.
This is precisely the correct explanation for the question: "Can one see the Tathāgata through signs?"
Therefore, Bodhisattva Devaśarman set forth twenty-seven doubts, which also begin from this point.

The old interpretation, which explains it as "one should give in this manner, not dwelling on signs," is even more remote. This is because it distinguishes the essence of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and prevents the attainment of its fulfillment;
since the three characteristics have distinct essences, that which is apart from them is the Tathāgata. This is the correct explanation of "if one sees..."
To see that all marks are no-marks is to behold the Tathāgata. Thus far, the subduing of the mind, non-abiding, and giving are all conditioned entities;
they are not the true Tathāgata, because they possess the distinctions of the three marks. The three marks are the Nirmāṇakāya, the Saṃbhogakāya, and the Dharmakāya.
Only when one sets aside the Saṃbhoga and Nirmāṇa bodies and alone manifests the Dharmakāya is it the true Tathāgata. This is the primary cause.

Since Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) refers to the Buddhas of the present as "Tathāgatas," [the text] specifically clarifies the distinctions between the three bodies (trikāya) to reveal the causal conditions of the three periods of time.
To claim that the speaker [Nāgārjuna] takes the practice of giving (*dāna*) and abiding [in precepts] as the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is also erroneous.

Generally speaking, the three bodies (trikāya) are not merely mentioned once. As it is said, "The response-body and transformation-body are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma.
Here, "response-body" specifically refers to the Tathāgatas of the past; it is in reliance upon that Dharma-body Buddha that the metaphor of the "great body" is taught.

The Dharma-body (dharmakāya) specifically refers to the Buddha of the present. This is because, when discussed in terms of form and appearance, the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) belongs to the past and the Response-body (saṃbhogakāya) belongs to the present, whereas the Dharma-body exists throughout the three periods of time.

However, when discussed in terms of the fundamental essence (svabhāva), both the Response-body and the Transformation-body belong to the past, while the Dharma-body belongs to the present. Therefore, it is stated below: "The ultimate essence of the Dharma-body is not that [of the other two]."

The body endowed with the primary and secondary marks refers to the Buddhas of the present; although they possess the Dharma-body, it is ultimately a physical form rather than the true Dharma-characteristic, because it is not accomplished through marks and is not that [true] Dharma-body.

As for the Tathāgatas of the past, although they possessed the Dharma-body, in the final analysis, it was likewise not the locus of the true Dharma. By speaking of "Buddha" and "Tathāgata" in pairs, he reveals [this distinction].
There are degrees of depth, yet they all converge in the single non-characteristic (*animitta*). Furthermore, none of them depart from the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*);

therefore, it is stated below that they do not depart from the *dharmakāya*. Since those two are not other than the Buddha, they are again described as "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), which is neither dual nor existent.
What is called "dual" refers precisely to the Buddha and the Tathāgata; hence, it is stated below: "As..."
The Buddha-dharma is likewise so. "Suchness" (tathatā) is precisely the Tathāgata; it is not that the word "such" (tatha) is a mere empty phrase.

Nowadays, because people do not distinguish between these two aspects—both of which are fully endowed with all marks—they consequently repeat them redundantly until they become lost in confusion, having no point of reference. Furthermore, it is said:
"The Tathāgata cannot be known by comparison with the marks of the physical body (*rūpakāya*); the Buddhas possess only the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)," as does a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).

These marks are not the true marks of the Tathāgata; yet, as they both abide within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), although their appearances are not one, their essence is not different.
This "going, coming, sitting, and reclining" actually refers to the present Buddha and should be understood as the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body).
Because it is viewed in contrast to the Tathāgata, it is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body). "Not one" directly corresponds to the two characters above; for indeed—
The Buddha’s discourse reaches this point, beginning with the clear recognition of the Tathāgata; hence it is said that he is neither one nor different. It is further stated:

"The manifestation of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) displays merit, yet it is not without inexhaustible merit. When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do not say, "This is a transformation body.

The above verses emphasize the relationship between the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). This is because the so-called three characteristics are distinct in substance;
it is the essential point that the three periods of time are one and the same Dharma. Furthermore, this is clearly and explicitly demonstrated as a final summary.
It is said: "One contemplates characteristics and consciousness; the vessel, the body, and the objects of enjoyment; as well as past and present phenomena, and likewise the future world.
One contemplates characteristics and enjoyment; one contemplates the three periods of time. Within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one attains stainless sovereignty.

This is stated in summary regarding the general purport of the three periods of time throughout the entire sutra, specifically concerning the contemplation of characteristics and consciousness. Regarding the correct [practice]:
Within the single dharma of the three periods of time, one attains the stainless and pure true Dharma.
