During the Ming dynasty, perhaps these sixty-two characters were originally absent. If the second [title] is "The Orthodox Tradition of the Mahāyāna," it takes the subduing of the mind as the entire substance of the Mahāyāna.
The third is titled "Sublime Practice Without Abiding," which designates the word "practice" (xing).
This has reached the very core of the essential meaning. The contemporary practice of explaining essence and function together is the ultimate discourse;
it is not an introductory exposition. The fourth section, "Seeing According to Reality," sufficiently marks the locus of the entire scripture’s central tenet.
It is vastly different from those who provide later generations with openings for the emergence of doubt. The eighteenth section, titled "Observing the Single Essence as Identical," is most...

One attains the principle of the single essence of the three periods of time. The twentieth [section] is titled "Detachment from Form and Detachment from Characteristics," which is particularly clear in its presentation of the two aspects of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) side by side.

The twenty-sixth is titled "The Dharma-Body is Without Characteristics," which singles out the two characters for "dharma-body" and provides an even more detailed analysis. The twenty-ninth states, "Dignified Manner and Tranquility," referring exclusively to the present...
In the teachings of Śākyamuni Buddha, one especially attains the causal conditions of the three periods of time. His manifestations over thirty-two days were provisional and not ultimate;

these too are explained from the perspective of the present Śākyamuni. Observing how he grasps the meaning with precision—where not a single word is taken lightly—it is clear that everything is derived from a thorough understanding of the entire scripture, reaching both its depths and its shallows.
This is by no means like a person of the present day who looks to the east and neglects the west, or gazes ahead while losing sight of what lies behind.

Later, [I realized that] it perfectly accords with the fundamental tenets of the Tathāgatas of the three periods and forms a complementary whole with the *Gāthās of Maitreya* regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Yet, people of today, because its structural divisions are somewhat loose, have simultaneously neglected the subtlety of its core meaning.

They recklessly claim that Zhaoming’s work is a fabrication—truly like the intimidation of a phoenix by a *yuanchu* bird, or the derision of a cicada or a swallow toward the great Peng. When I first read it, I too was quite [skeptical].

I realized that my own efforts were fragmentary and insufficient to rely upon. Only after completing my studies did I come to know that Gaoxin had preceded me, like the sound of footsteps in an empty valley.
I have therefore placed his verses alongside those of Maitreya at the beginning of this work to serve as a means for cross-referential verification.
As for other scholars whose works sufficiently capture the true character of the sūtra’s text, I have selected one or two; in total, I do not wish to merely [accumulate citations].
To boast of one's vast learning is to deceive the ears and eyes of others.
Regarding the treatises of the two Bodhisattvas, Asaṅga and Vasubandhu, which have been most highly revered in recent times, their commentaries originally derive from the verses of Maitreya;
yet they do not always accord perfectly with them. Perhaps this is because each of these divine sages manifested his own particular insight.
It is so. One need not be strictly bound by outward forms or literal traces.

As for the twenty-seven points for severing doubt, because the scriptural text is circuitous and lacks clear markers, making its divisions difficult to discern, I have therefore traced them from the underlying reasons for the establishment of the discourse.
Thus, these twenty-seven layers of causal conditions for generating the resolve were extracted; indeed, ordinary sentient beings ought to possess such [resolves].

Because various doubts and difficulties arise, [the Buddha] uses the dialogue between Subhūti and himself to reveal and clarify them. People today rely too heavily on external precedents and, conversely, lose the essential intent of the sūtra;

therefore, I shall briefly set forth the general meaning to serve as a reference. For instance, regarding the initial doubt concerning the cessation of the mark of abiding in the practice of giving while seeking Buddhahood:
it is argued that practicing giving is a truly real function, so how could it be "without marks"? Furthermore—
Since it is said "dwelling," this clearly refers to the language of stages and positions. How could ordinary people not be perplexed?

Therefore, he next asks about the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata’s body. For while the physical marks are forms that possess shape, the Tathāgata remains ever-present even as those forms undergo transformation;
thus, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) characterized by functional utility are insufficient to be retained. This is the principle.
It is merely this. Yet those who speak claim that practicing giving with the primary aim of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood constitutes a "mark" (nimitta);

this adds an extra layer of complication and, conversely, results in obscurity. As for the claim that practicing giving while abiding therein corresponds to the three marks within Maitreya’s verses—how could the two characters for "practicing giving" (*dāna*) be split into two separate marks?
Both the negation [of marks] and the cause-and-effect [relationship] are profound and difficult to believe.
Question: The physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are the signs of practice on the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), whereas the Tathāgata is the fruition of the present dharma-marks.
One who can see the mark that is no-mark sees the Tathāgata; thus, both cause and fruit are profound.
Yet, the speaker takes giving and abiding as the cause and the Buddha-marks as the fruit. If one can practice in this way, one will naturally become a Buddha—what difficulty is there in this?

[Subhūti] says: "It is not fitting for one born of emptiness to come to such a vulgar and limited [view]. Although the Buddha preaches the Dharma for ordinary people, he would certainly not hold a shallow view to this extent.
Regarding the third [point], the severance of the signless (*animitta*), how can doubt be spoken of? The *Jiejie* (Explanatory Commentary) states that some say:
"One cannot see the Buddha by means of bodily marks (*lakṣaṇa*). This is the statement of Subhūti; how could he give rise to doubt regarding his own words?
Regarding the doubt: this refers to the concern that future sentient beings might harbor such doubts; one must not be overly rigid on this point.

This may be called a skillful way of interpreting Vasubandhu’s resolution of doubts. In my humble opinion, what is meant by "signlessness" (animitta) is precisely the aforementioned "absence of the marks of dharmas" (dharma-lakṣaṇa).
Since there are no marks of dharmas, for what reason do all Tathāgatas preach the Dharma? Therefore, the following [text] uses "existence" [to address this].
There are those who claim that this cannot be refuted. Their argument traces back to the statement that the Tathāgata is "not seen.
They ask: how could Śākyamuni have attained the Dharma and preached it beneath the Bodhi tree?

Furthermore, as for the title "Tathāgata" used here, when has a Buddha ever willingly identified himself as such? The four types of abandonment and the śrāvakas' attainment of the fruits are based on doubt.
The preceding passage stated that all teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are neither graspable nor expressible.

Fearing that people might suspect that the Mahāyāna taught by the Tathāgata is ungraspable while the Śrāvaka-yāna taught below it might be graspable, [the text] further corroborates this with each of the four fruits of the śrāvakas, as well as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, so that one may see that the essential meaning is that all are ungraspable. Furthermore, the speaker says:

1. To resolve the doubt that the *sūtra* text originally states that the *srotāpanna* and others each attain their respective fruits and speak according to their realization, yet [the commentary] adds a further layer before this.
2. To resolve the doubt that the fivefold abandonment contradicts the teaching that Śākyamuni and Dīpaṃkara attained [the fruit].
3. To resolve the doubt that there is a contradiction regarding the reception of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Regarding the "taking up" of doubt: the essential purport of all three doubts returns to the chapter on "non-appropriation.

When the light of correct vision shines far and wide and the channels of principle are clear and penetrating, one sees that the scriptural passage beginning with "Therefore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...

should be understood as a collective response to the six questions. However, the commentator has divided it according to the three doubts and treated each separately as a distinct heading for elaboration. That is to say:
Once one has turned three bends, one no longer recognizes the path ahead. If we take the two characters "ru" (如) and "bi" (譬) as examples, they should properly be understood as metaphors.
Yet, Vasubandhu actually realized the *sambhogakāya* (retribution body), deriving his meaning from the perspective of ultimate reality. People today, however, remain mired in literal interpretations;
even after eight times of reciting and explaining [the text], they have not yet escaped the doubt regarding the fruit of suffering. This refers precisely to Subhūti in the original chapter.
He wept and wailed in grief. Seeing this most rare and extraordinary Dharma, he felt that it was improper to continue to cling to the marks of body and life;
thus, from the passage "The foremost is not foremost" downward, [the text] closely follows with the teaching on "patience and non-patience" to awaken him.
Yet the speaker has instead become entangled in distant external wealth, comparing its excellence and thereby inducing the suffering of humans and devas.

The words "fruit" and so forth are likewise merely entanglements. The ninth [point], "proving that there is no substance, which is not a cause for doubt," means that "no substance" is precisely what the Maitreya verse calls the "Way" (*mārga*).
This refers to the two instances of the word "says" (*āha*) in the preceding passage:
"The Tathāgata says that all marks are non-marks" and "he says that all sentient beings are non-sentient beings. These two instances of the word "says" are the word "Way. That is, it is non-existent.
The Master [Xuanzang] feared that people might doubt the statement regarding "no-substance" (anātman/nirvastuka), thinking it could not serve as a cause for realizing the fruit of enlightenment;

therefore, he clarified this below by means of the four kinds of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). However, the commentator has gone to great lengths to maintain the integrity of the scripture and engage in comparative analysis, which is truly unnecessary.
Regarding the ten abandonments, such as "existence," "non-existence," "attainment," "non-attainment," and "doubt," they proceed from the statement above:
"this dharma is neither real nor unreal. "Neither real nor unreal" refers to the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the four kinds of wisdom mentioned above.

Since it is beyond substantiality and verbal expression, yet possesses such a true mark, would one not say that everyone can attain it? Nevertheless, this is not the case unless the mind abides [in stillness].
One must practice it with sincerity. Though one may hear the words and believe them, what ultimate benefit is there?

Therefore, the following clarifies both practicing with the mind abiding and practicing with the mind not abiding. Furthermore, the phrase "at that time, he spoke, far transcending all noble and holy ones" is not necessarily required.
[The commentary states: "The eleventh [section] concerns the doubt: 'Is it by abandoning, abiding, cultivating, or subduing? No, for non-self is certainly the theme of this chapter."

The purport of this chapter is as follows: However, since this is based on the intention behind Śāriputra’s repeated questioning regarding the existence of distinct characteristics, the word "self" (ātman) is singled out for discussion.
Thus, it is also unimpeded to seek and explain this in detail from the standpoint of ultimate reality.

For the Buddha’s words are inherently versatile and multifaceted; one need not be overly rigid. Therefore, when Maitreya (Vasubandhu) resolved doubts, he likewise spoke from the standpoint of ultimate reality. Nevertheless, it must...
Bodhi asked again: "It is merely that you suspect there is a difference between the Buddha and the Tathāgata; in truth, there is no view of self within your breast.
Yet the speaker has concluded that Subhūti harbors doubts. Since there is no self, who is it that descends and abides?"
Who is it that practices? To lift up my name before one would be like engaging in forced interpretation.

Because there is doubt regarding Bodhi within the "Twelve Cessations of the Buddha," and because the preceding text states that "in reality, there is no dharma," people may fear this and doubt whether the Buddha was unable to be without Bodhi during his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).
The character "提" (ti) has been erroneously changed to "薩" (sa) in the current edition; furthermore—
This is for the sake of further clarification. It is not that the preceding text states there are four characteristics and therefore one is not a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma that gives rise to the bodhicitta. From this point onward, it clearly explains in truth that there is no bodhicitta;
how could this be the character *sa* (the first syllable of *bodhisattva*)? [Section] Thirteen: Severing the doubt that if there are no causes, there can be no Buddha-dharma. Regarding "no cause":
If the Bodhi of the ground were likewise devoid of the present Buddha-dharma, then [the text] subsequently explains it by means of the names of the Tathāgatas.
This is because not only is the present Buddha thus, but all past Tathāgatas are likewise so.
Therefore, all dharmas of all Tathāgatas are the Buddha-dharma. At this point, the Buddha himself—
The Tathāgata Mingxing (Manifesting Radiance) possesses but a single Dharma; therefore, within the section on severing doubts, he also points out the two characters "Buddha-Dharma.

Fourteenth is the severing of the doubt that there is no person to save sentient beings or adorn the lands. This word "person" follows from the previous analogy, "It is like a person whose body is vast and great.
Since this great body is not a great body, this person is also not a person. Who then will save sentient beings? Who will adorn [the lands]?

To adorn the Buddha-lands. One must know that this "person" (pudgala) is not a person in the sense of a self; rather, it is the very meaning of the word "person. Therefore, the text below clarifies this by stating:
"I shall bring sentient beings to extinction" and "I shall adorn the Buddha-lands"—if one holds such views, they are clearly not Bodhisattvas.
Fifteenth, severing the doubt that the Buddhas do not perceive all phenomena: this follows from the aforementioned teaching of non-self (*anātman*).

This is the true Bodhisattva who comes. To say that those who adorn themselves with the thought of saving sentient beings are not Bodhisattvas, while one who is without self or dharmas is a true Bodhisattva—does this not mean that all Buddhas do not perceive the existence of any dharmas?

Therefore, the text below clarifies this by showing that the mind of the three periods of time is unobtainable. Since the mind does not perceive the three periods, the Buddha likewise does not perceive any [dharmas].
The Dharma is precisely the true principle; yet the Buddha and the Tathāgata are one with this Dharma, which remains implicitly present beyond words.
Regarding the sixteenth [section], "Eliminating Doubts Concerning the Inversion of the Mind Regarding Merit": "Inversion" refers to the conventional mind.
If it is said that the three minds are unattainable, how could it be that the karmic retribution is also unattainable? One cannot help but harbor doubt; therefore, the following [text] uses...
Virtue and merit lack substantial reality; this is clarified by the necessity of seeing that the abundance of virtue and merit exists precisely because they have no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Thus, it is not the case that the Bodhisattva Dharmadhātu lacks true virtue and merit, and through this, the mind of perversion can also be severed.

(17) [This concludes] the severing of the doubt as to why there are marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) if there is non-existence. In the preceding text, it was stated that there is no self, no dharmas, no two time periods, and no virtue.

Virtues are all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Since it is thus stated that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent, why does the Buddha possess the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), and why does the Tathāgata possess the various marks of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)? To speak of both together reveals their relative shallowness and depth.
The doubts of the common masses all converge upon this single point; therefore, to sever these doubts, they are also addressed collectively. Yet, the speaker has treated them as a whole...
Master Yi-fu examined this and forcibly attempted to allocate the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) and thirty-two primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) according to Vasubandhu’s treatise.

He failed to realize that Vasubandhu’s treatise also speaks of these in general terms; it never actually divided them. Both the eighty secondary marks and the thirty-two primary marks are all *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics).
How could there be any distinction between them? Furthermore, since the eighteen emptinesses (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*) are without body (*anātman*), how can they be said to preach the Dharma?
Question: Since it is stated that there are no marks of the three bodies (*trikāya*), how can they still preach the Dharma while in the world?

This is likely intended to completely negate even the act of preaching the Dharma within the context of non-existence. Therefore, the following clarifies this by stating that "there is no dharma that can be explained. Vasubandhu says:
If the marks and signs of the Tathāgata’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) cannot be perceived, how can it be said that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma?
This is precisely the point: the proponent [of the opposing view] argues that since there is no form-body, from where could sound issue?

Thus, they take what is actually non-existent and insist upon treating it as if it were an existent phenomenon. (19) How to resolve the doubt regarding the cultivation and realization of non-existence: this follows from the above.
If all phenomena are entirely non-existent, then how should one practice and realize Buddhahood in the present?
This is precisely an intimate inquiry concerning the Buddha of the present. Therefore, while the preceding passage refers to the Tathāgata, this one refers specifically to the Buddha.

Previously, the question was posed with both the perspectives of "attainment" and "non-attainment" concurrently; here, the question is asked with exclusive focus on the single perspective that "attainment" is itself "non-attainment. This is precisely [the point].
To provide a path for those who doubt how to practice and realize [the goal], this is a definitive (nītārtha) teaching; it is fundamentally different from what preceded it.
As Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "If the Tathāgata does not attain even a single dharma, it is called unsurpassed bodhi.
How can one, apart from the supreme realization, progressively attain unsurpassed bodhi? What is called "unsurpassed bodhi" precisely refers to this.
The term "attainment" is used [here] to mean "non-attainment. The light of the eye is extremely subtle.
What is called "transcending the supreme realization to further attain the unsurpassed" explains how to cultivate and realize; it is also one level higher.

When the commentator further uses expressions such as "the third" or "the tenth," it is directly stated that bodhi cannot be attained. This is due to a failure in parsing the text. It is not [as some claim].
This is because [the Buddha] knows the depth and shallowness [of their capacities]. Regarding the twenty points concerning the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states taught as being non-causes for doubt:
the previous statement that "by cultivating all wholesome dharmas one attains Bodhi" was intended to mean upholding and expounding this sutra;

yet [those states] are ultimately of an indeterminate nature, or perhaps not bound by cause and effect. Therefore, the text below again compares them in terms of the superiority of merit. However, this too is a skillful [expedient means].

This is the "Arising and Development. It serves as a guide for future generations. If one were to discuss the scriptural text itself, each section is indeed concluded with a statement on the superior merit of the practice;
yet it is not necessarily so restrictive. Commentators should also understand this well and must not adhere to it dogmatically. Twenty-one:
Resolving the doubt regarding how to save sentient beings through the equality of severance. It says that since sentient beings are equal, they all possess...

Regarding the Buddha-nature, why would it be necessary for the Tathāgata to further deliver sentient beings? What follows below uses the reality that there is truly no one to be delivered as a supporting proof;
this is precisely the explanation from the first chapter stating, "In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.

Yet, some commentators claim that the Tathāgata’s delivery of sentient beings actually involves degrees of superiority and inferiority and is truly unequal. This greatly deviates from the intent of the Sūtra. (22)
To sever the doubt regarding the true Buddha by means of comparison and to contemplate the Tathāgata through signs is like mistaking a sheep for a tiger;
how could such comparison equal true knowledge? Therefore, the analogy of a wheel-turning monarch is used to awaken one to this. Contemplation (*guan*) and seeing (*jian*) are not the same;

thus, it specifically says "knowledge" (*zhi*). Those who explain this fail to realize the difference in depth between contemplation and seeing, and continue to speak of the marks and signs of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
To repeat this over and over again is nothing more than scratching an itch through a boot. [Section] Twenty-three: Doubting that the Buddha-fruit is unrelated to the marks of merit.
Building upon the previous statement that one may observe within the marks, this could be called a subtle point;
yet even this is not permissible. If so, then the Buddha-fruit is entirely without marks. Indeed, the entire scripture refutes and strips away anything that is not the markless.
This is simply that not even a single hair’s breadth of thought should be attached; how then could the doubt of "stubborn emptiness" (wánkōng) not arise?

Therefore, [the text] immediately follows this by defining it as "not forming the mark of annihilation. Yet, commentators have further conflated this with the retribution of merit and blessings, thereby obscuring the intent of the Sūtra.
[Section] Twenty-four: Dispelling the Doubt Regarding the Appearance of Transformation Bodies (nirmāṇakāya) to Receive Blessings. The preceding text states:
This bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the preceding bodhisattvas; they are what are called the "bodhisattvas who currently preach the Dharma.

Therefore, it is said that "an emanation body appears. In the following text, the Buddha also clarifies this by using the present, past, and future, as well as sitting and reclining, to illustrate it.
One must understand that although those who currently preach the Dharma are emanation bodies, they nevertheless still possess the true Dharmakāya.

If [the Buddha] is present, is it not fitting that he should receive merit? Yet, since it is said that a Bodhisattva should receive merit, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) would be no different from the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, since it is also said that [the Buddha] comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, the dharma-body and the transformation body are again not one.
Is this not a cause for doubt? Therefore, the twenty-fifth [verse] says: "The dharma-body is severed."

There arises doubt regarding whether the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is identical to or distinct from [the dharmakāya]. However, the subsequent text clarifies this through the true principle of the phenomenal world (*dharmadhātu*).
One must recognize that the perception of a distinction between the transformation body and the dharma-body arises from the arising of views regarding the phenomenal world.

If such views concerning the phenomenal world are extinguished, what distinction would there then be between the Dharma and its transformations? At this point, the Buddha and the Tathāgata are a single reality throughout the three periods of time; the entire matter has been set forth.
Having brought this forth, the expositor still does not realize the principle of the three periods of time.

Not knowing where terms such as "transformation body" (nirmāṇakāya) and "dharma body" (dharmakāya) are to be applied, one observes that these twenty-seven doubts are in fact complementary to Maitreya’s verses, yet the expositor remains muddled.
This concludes the twenty-sixth [section], which resolves the doubt that the transformation body’s preaching of the Dharma lacks merit.
It is said that a Bodhisattva ought to receive blessings. Why, then, should there be further doubt that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) lacks blessings?
This is because the sense that [the Bodhisattva] should receive blessings—whether departing or arriving—is truly intended beyond the literal words; it was not explicitly stated.

Furthermore, since the subsequent chapter states that knowledge, vision, faith, and understanding all do not give rise to the marks of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa), one consequently doubts the teaching regarding the transformation body.
The Dharma possesses no [inherent] merit. Below, this is clarified by means of the most supreme merit.
Yet, this most supreme merit resides solely in suchness (*tathatā*), which is non-apprehension of signs. Why is this? Because the true dharma of the Tathāgata is thus.
This single phrase is the essential purport of the entire sutra and its complete summary; the four lines of verse that follow merely explicate this.
I understand. However, fearing that the common masses might not comprehend this, I have simply taken *nirvāṇa* (寂滅) as *tathatā* (如如).
Therefore, I have further brought forth verses to clarify this. These verses precisely discern the signless (*animitta*) from within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
This is not a matter of merely relying on the one-sidedness of non-action (*wuwei*). Therefore, the twenty-seventh doubt asks: "How can one who has entered quiescence (*jì*) give rise to doubt?
To understand the meaning of the verse regarding *tathatā* (suchness), it is clearly not a case of entering quiescence into a state of inert emptiness (*wánkōng*).
As Vasubandhu said: "If all Buddhas and Tathāgatas constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, how is it that the Tathāgata enters *nirvāṇa*?"
This is also spoken for the sake of those of common and shallow understanding. The speaker thus uses the two characters "nirvāṇa" to truly express the unmoving suchness (*tathatā*).
Yet, they further use "stubborn emptiness" (*wánkōng*) to explain the verse. Those who do not understand this and harbor doubts must precisely reverse their views.
If one uses "stubborn emptiness" to explain the verse, it is simply entering into quiescence without preaching the Dharma.

This is certainly not intended to dispel doubts. As I examine these twenty-seven doubts, I see that they are specifically designed for ordinary people to seek a gate and find a path—to extract a thread from amidst a lack of threads.
There is a profound sincerity in every section; when one reflects upon them in light of the preceding text, they are entirely free of digression or complexity.
I did not expect that later generations would go to such lengths in their forced interpretations, abandoning what is near to seek what is far.
Consequently, the scriptural text has been rendered obscure. It is truly as if the "Xing and He" swords have been cast away and precious blades covered in dust;

were it not for those with discernment, who could rectify this? While the various doubts I harbor are indeed unavoidable for ordinary minds, they ultimately cannot be divided into mere chapters, sections, or paragraphs.
If one relies upon them as if they were walls, only more complications will ensue; therefore, I did not dare to record them.

However, in recent times, those who expound upon the teachings have come to regard this as their highest veneration; thus, I have categorized the passages of the scripture alongside each section for the convenience of students to consult.
The Buddha-dharma cannot be sought through written words; it is said that it is not like the pedantic deliberations and literary carvings of a scholar.
To refine words and phrases is "craft" (*gōng*); to apply tonal patterns and rhymes is "style" (*gé*).
As for the sequential order of preceding and following sections and their mutual resonance in terms of depth, this is the natural principle of the mind’s resonance (*xīnshēng*).

Even among worldly people who have a slight understanding of literary meaning, when they speak or converse, there is invariably a sequence of beginning and conclusion, with preceding and following parts resonating with one another; how much more so for the Divine and the Spirit!
O Sage! From the tip of a single hair, you release the worlds of devas and humans;
yet to claim that these secret texts and numinous images merely expound upon Prajñāpāramitā is, on the contrary, no different from the admonitions of an old woman or the clamor of a village rustic.
This is what I most dare not believe. Master Lianchi said: "The words of the Vajra [Sūtra] seem weighty, yet they are not weighty; they are not weighty."

Furthermore, it is profound and extremely difficult to annotate. The *Vajra-Right-Eye* states: Regarding the sections following the seventeenth, various masters have offered different interpretations.
Some say that what was previously discussed was not yet exhaustive; some say it concerns the coarse and subtle aspects of our own Dharma;
some say it is a repeated inquiry regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta; some say it involves non-humans who do not manifest themselves; and some say it cites others as being oneself.
As for those who grasp at handles, they are all merely speaking dreams within a dream; this is truly the language for repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Reflect on it:
the original text of the sutra says, "Upon hearing these chapters and phrases, one should accept, uphold, read, recite, and explain them to others.

Thus, when the Buddha preached this sutra, there were originally its own chapters and phrases that could be understood and explained. Why, then, do you instead pursue the wind and bind shadows? Each [of you]...

This is merely the indulgence of my own arbitrary views. I maintain that this sutra, in its circular phrasing and the interplay between restraint and release, possesses a depth and gradation of levels such that it is, in every stroke, a most disciplined and well-ordered composition, much like the *Great Learning* and the *Doctrine of the Mean*.
For now, I shall briefly set forth my humble observations. "If one sees the markless mark, then one sees the Tathāgata"—this single phrase is indeed the central purport of the entire sutra.
It perfectly corresponds in meaning with the final verse, "Abiding in suchness, immovable.
"Abiding in suchness, immovable" is precisely the markless mark. All conditioned phenomena...

One should contemplate in this manner; then one sees the Tathāgata. This is like the Kunlun Mountains and Lake Anavatapta being in breath-like resonance with the great ocean’s tail-gate (the outflow). Apart from this, there is no so-called "other shore.

Since the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally beyond the reach of the ears and eyes, it cannot be seen. This meaning is also quite simple and direct, yet compared to the initial question regarding the *rūpakāya*, it is more profound.

This refers to what is called "the severance of anger. However, it is the foremost meaning of being "rare" (āścarya), and since one can also "surpass" it, we know that within the meaning of "rare," the severance of anger is already included;

At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and addressed the Buddha, saying:

World-Honored One, if there should be another person who hears this sutra and their mind of faith becomes pure, then the mark of reality will arise. You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit. World-Honored One, this mark of reality is..."

"It is not a mark. For this reason, the Tathāgata calls it the 'true mark. World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.

Why? Subhūti, what the Tathāgata calls the foremost *pāramitā* is, in fact, not the foremost *pāramitā*; it is named the foremost *pāramitā*. Subhūti, as for the *pāramitā* of patience...”
This is not called the perfection of patience. Why is this? Subhūti, when in the past King Kali cut and mangled my body, at that time—

They come to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this? A single source. If scholars can depart from verbal signs through words and transcend speech, they may perhaps attain it.

This section consists of Subhūti’s renewed inquiry regarding the present Buddha-dharma, to which the Buddha replies that there is no "self" in the dharma. Previously, Subhūti had been inquiring about the Buddha-dharma in general;

however, because the Buddha repeatedly referred to the Tathāgata, Subhūti suspected that the Buddha possessed some distinct dharma of his own. It is only upon reaching this point that he directs his question specifically toward the good sons and good daughters of the present age.

Now, because Subhūti suspected the Buddha might be something distinct, the Buddha drew them closer together.

The true Dharma-characteristic is precisely signlessness. Zongle’s commentary states: The intent of the question is to ask whether one may perceive the characteristics of the *dharmakāya* within the physical marks and refinements of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
"No. It is precisely this meaning. (23.

Dispelling the Doubt that the Buddha-fruit is Not Related to Auspicious Marks) "Subhūti, if you should have such a thought: 'The Tathāgata did not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the possession of marks,' Subhūti, do not have such a thought.
The Tathāgata did not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the possession of marks. Subhūti, if you should have such..."
Do not think thus: "One who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speaks of the annihilation and extinction of all phenomena. Why is this?
One who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.

This section states that although the Tathāgata is without marks (*animitta*), he is nevertheless not a mark of annihilation. This is precisely the meaning of being neither a dharma-mark nor a non-dharma-mark. Whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he necessarily encompasses both the meanings of existence and non-existence;

therefore, the text alternates between sweeping away and saving, and between saving and sweeping away. For instance, in the first chapter: "Whatever marks there may be, they are all illusory" is a sweeping away (*sao*);

"If one sees that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata" is a saving (*jiu*). In the second chapter: "One should not grasp at dharmas" is a sweeping away; "one should not grasp at non-dharmas" is a saving.

The tone of the entire sutra is consistently of this nature. Nevertheless, it has never explicitly stated that there is a specific location [where one enters]. This is because it is easy for the human mind to leave non-existence and enter existence, whereas it is difficult to leave existence and enter non-existence.
Therefore, at this particular point—when the Tathāgata’s ultimate state of being without dharma and without marks is specifically reiterated—the text speaks clearly to people, saying:

"I do not speak of the mark of annihilation. The intent behind establishing this teaching is profound and perfect. Thus, Zongle said: "Regarding the causes of merit cultivated in the Mahāyāna and the merit obtained..."
The fruit is merely the state of being free from the marks of grasping; it is not like the view of annihilation held by the Lesser Vehicle.

Truly so, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them in charity, yet another person were to know that all dharmas are without self and thereby achieve patient endurance (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva would surpass the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhūti, it is because these bodhisattvas do not accept [the accumulation of] blessings.

Because of this virtue, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit? “Subhūti, the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be clung to with greed;
for this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit.”

This section speaks of the ultimate karmic reward of the Tathāgata’s Dharma. The various karmic rewards mentioned previously were referred to as "people" in the chapter on "Faith Without Grasping," marking the beginning of understanding.

The rest are all referred to as "good sons" and "good daughters," which pertains to the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*). Only the opening chapter and this [passage] refer to them as "Bodhisattvas";

this is because they speak in relation to the Dharma of the Tathāgata, representing the exhaustion of understanding and the perfection of practice. Such is the difference between the preceding and following sections. "No-self" (*anātman*) refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). "Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

"Attaining perfection in patience" refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) within the unconditioned. This statement also encompasses both existence and non-existence; for it is easy for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to maintain existence, but difficult to maintain non-existence. A Bodhisattva...

For one who is about to achieve Buddhahood through study, maintaining [the state of non-existence] is easy, while maintaining [the state of existence] is difficult. Therefore it is said: "Success is attained through patience; maintaining existence within non-existence cannot be accomplished without patience. This principle is most subtle. Thus the verse says:

"Attaining supreme patience and not losing it, one thereby attains the stainless fruit. Following the teaching of non-self, one attains supremacy; this is true supremacy. True supremacy does not cling to any single side.
At this time, to maintain it through the power of patience without losing it is the very accomplishment of the Buddha-fruit. Its merit naturally surpasses that of all other bodhisattvas.

Indeed. This is precisely the juncture where, according to the Confucian tradition, utmost sincerity is unceasing and after a long duration manifests its signs. In this scripture, it serves as the true commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and the *śarīra* (relic) of the entire sutra;

it emerges specifically at the point where the Tathāgata’s Dharma is exhausted. It is like a dragon from a thousand miles away that settles its "vortex" here. It does not accept blessings, for it lacks the marks of merit.

Furthermore, because one should not greedily cling to them, the sense that "merit is great" is left to be understood beyond the words. This is because one who has already become a Bodhisattva is free from anger.
Ignorance is easily severed, but craving alone is difficult to avoid. Where there is grasping and acquisition, all is craving; therefore, it is compared to the superiority of wealth and treasures.
Furthermore, by singling out the precept against attachment to craving, the "fine needle within the cotton" reveals a profound intention.
The above constitutes the sixth chapter of the sutra, stating that the Tathāgata is without marks (*animitta*) and yet not without marks.

(24. Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Appearance of the Nirmāṇakāya and the Receiving of Merit) Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.

Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. (25. Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Identity or Difference between the Dharmakāya and the Nirmāṇakāya) Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with [a world-system of] three thousand great thousand worlds...
“If this world were ground into atoms, what do you think? Would that multitude of atoms be numerous? “Very numerous, World-Honored One. Why is this?

If that multitude of atoms existed as a reality, the Buddha would not have spoken of it as a ‘multitude of atoms. For what reason? That which the Buddha calls a ‘multitude of atoms’ is not a multitude of atoms;

it is merely designated as a ‘multitude of atoms. World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata calls a ‘trichiliocosm’ is not a world; it is merely designated as a ‘world. Why is this? If a world were real...”

That which exists is a "unified whole" (*piṇḍagraha*). The Tathāgata has said that a unified whole is not a unified whole; it is merely designated as a "unified whole. Subhūti, a unified whole is inexpressible;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things. (The character for "clinging" [zhuó] is pronounced zháo.)

This section states that the Buddha cannot be sought through marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Since it was already clarified above that the Tathāgata is without marks and is not a mark of annihilation, the following further states that the Buddha is without marks and is also not a view of the four marks of annihilation.

This is because they both ultimately converge in the Tathāgata, who is the Buddha of the markless-mark. Only upon reaching this point do [the marks of] coming, going, sitting, and lying down become manifest;

furthermore, these are spoken of in terms of the present. This is because coming, going, sitting, and lying down in the present are matters of the physical body (*rūpakāya*), and the physical body is the Tathāgata’s emanation (*nirmāṇakāya*).

This, however, is not the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata; the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata truly has no coming or going. Thus, a verse says: "The Buddhas who come and go are transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya); the Tathāgata is eternally unmoving.

Since the Buddha is thus a transformation body of the Tathāgata, he truly exists within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Although his body is not identical with that of the Tathāgata, it is also not different from it.

Therefore, the verse says: "In this realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), it is neither one nor different. However, the meaning of these two lines does not appear in the scriptural text; rather, Maitreya provided them specifically because he feared people might doubt that the Buddha is actually distinct from the Tathāgata.

In short, although the Buddha did not speak of it himself, it is nonetheless implied by his intent. The world being shattered into subtle atoms (paramāṇu) is a metaphorical expression for the Dharmakāya manifesting as the Nirmāṇakāya. Thus, the *Jijie* states:

"The 'realm' (dhātu) is a metaphor for the True Body (Svabhāvakāya), and the 'atoms' are a metaphor for the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya). It is not that the subtle atoms themselves [are the True Body]."

What is called a "minute particle" (*paramāṇu*) is not a world, yet it is called a world; this is like saying that what is not a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is called a transformation body, or that what is not the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is called the dharma-body.

For in the Buddha-dharma, all is but mind. Minute particles and worlds are all formed through the conjunction of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); they do not exist apart from the mind. Since minute particles and worlds are empty, where then would the dharma-body and the transformation body be?

Therefore, to be able to not produce the appearance of a world is precisely the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); only then can one truly see the Tathāgata. This means that sentient beings harbor doubts regarding the Buddha.

The notions of coming and going arise solely from the view that the world is broken down into atoms of dust. If one can know that the world is not a world and that atoms are not atoms, then one can realize the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If one can know that coming and going are not coming and going, then the true mark of the Buddha exists therein. "A single unified mark" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) refers to a mark of conjunction;

it is here that the Buddha clearly identifies himself as the Tathāgata and explicitly tells those sentient beings that they must not cling to the marks of coming and going, but should recognize the Tathāgata.
Come. This further uses the world and its constituent atoms as real dharmas to provide proof; thus, the Buddha truly possesses no marks of self.
Therefore, this section should not be viewed in contrast with the previous section on "viewing the Tathāgata through marks," for their structural arrangement is naturally so.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span, what do you think, Subhūti?
Would such a person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One; such a person would not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why is this?

World-Honored One, when the Buddha speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span, these are not actually views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; they are merely designated as the "view of a self," the "view of a person," the "view of a sentient being," and the "view of a life-span. Subhūti...

“O Bodhi! Those who have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should, regarding all dharmas, know them thus, see them thus, and believe and understand them thus, so that no mark of dharma arises.
Subhūti, what is called the ‘mark of dharma’ has been taught by the Tathāgata as not being a mark of dharma; it is merely designated as the ‘mark of dharma.’”

This section states that although the Buddha has no marks of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), it does not mean he holds the nihilistic view that sentient beings and so forth truly do not exist; nor does it imply that he possesses a mental state characterized by non-phenomena (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*).

The characters "seeing" (jiàn) and "characteristics" (xiàng) are not the same. "Characteristics" refers to contact; "seeing" refers to the nature [of phenomena]. Because the preceding chapter stated that a "unified characteristic" (yīhéxiàng) cannot be spoken of, there may be those who suspect that the Buddha intends the four characteristics to be annihilated.

They fail to realize that the Buddha precisely takes the non-existence of the four characteristics as the four characteristics; it is through this that he is able to deliver sentient beings and achieve Buddhahood. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

"The five aggregates are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true suchness-nature. If one were necessarily intent on annihilating the view of the four characteristics, setting them aside, then apart from these four characteristics, what else would there be for a Buddha?

Therefore it is said: "This is called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span. This meaning is in fact contrasted with the notion of annihilationism (*uccheda*).

To know thus is to know that there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. To see thus is to see that there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. To believe and understand thus is to believe and understand that there is neither dharma nor non-dharma.

Although the text concludes here by referring solely to the Buddha-dharma, its meaning actually encompasses the three periods of time. Therefore, it is consistent with the fact that the past mind cannot be apprehended and the present mind...

It cannot be apprehended. The future mind cannot be apprehended. It is in correspondence [with reality]: the Right View of the Buddha and the Tathāgata is neither one nor two. Sentient beings and the Buddha are equal, without high or low.
This is what is called the true Dharma of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. When the Buddha had spoken thus, the eight jars of *śarīra* were brought forth upon a single platter.

Yet, fearing that people might still cling to biased views, he further used the mark of non-arising to seal the mark of emptiness, and again used the mark of non-dharmas to define the mark of dharmas, thus bringing it forth once more.

The ultimate truth. Both the words and their meanings are refined; both principle and phenomena are fully realized. Far-reaching, it illuminates the distant; near at hand, it responds to the immediate. In the void there is a subtle pulse;

in the substantial there is a solid thread. If dispersed, every single point is the Way; if unified, all returns to a single source. Viewed coarsely, it appears as successive segments; examined with precision, it is a seamless whole from beginning to end.
It is the supreme pattern of Heaven and Earth, the marvelous brushwork of the divine spirit.

(26. Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Lack of Merit in the Emanation Body Preaching the Dharma) Subhūti, if someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offer them as a gift, and if there were a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta (concluding the seventeenth section on the present question of the bodhisattvas) and, holding this sutra—even so much as a four-line verse—upholds, recites, and explains it to others, their merit would surpass that of the former. Why is this?

He expounds the Dharma for others, yet does not grasp at signs; he remains as suchness, unmoving. (27. Severing Doubts Regarding How to Expound the Dharma upon Entering Quiescence) Why is this? All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow;
they are like dew and also like lightning—one should contemplate them in this way.

This section speaks of the ultimate fruition of the Buddha-dharma, and by means of an ancient verse, it brings forth the true dharma of the entire sutra. The Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time penetrates from the highest to the lowest;
therefore, it is compared as being superior even to immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* acts of giving. *Asaṃkhyeya* refers to an incalculable number of kalpas.

"The Bodhisattva mind" refers to the truly Bodhisattva mind mentioned in the preceding chapter. Why is the merit so vast? It is because one who possesses the empty aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā*) expounds the dharma of the empty aspect of True Suchness.

Suchness is the one nature of true permanence. That which exists exists; that which does not exist does not exist. It is entirely without fabrication, purely and truly tranquil. When the mind is tranquil, wisdom arises.

When one’s nature is tranquil, attainment is reached; that is to say, when the water of meditative concentration is clear and still, the jewel of the mind manifests of itself. Indeed, only those who can truly possess this Dharma are subsequently able to expound it.

Is it not fitting, then, that their merit and virtue should be so great? This corresponds to the meaning of what is said in the *Zhongyong*: "If one is not inherently possessed of intelligence, sagacity, and wisdom, and has not attained the Virtue of Heaven, who then could know [this]?

Thus, the verse says: "The blessings manifested by the transformation body are not without inexhaustible merit. When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do not say, 'This is a transformation body'; yet whenever they speak, there must be the Dharma."

Only after [realizing] the body can one preach the Dharma. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—that is to say, all phenomena characterized by marks—are contrasted with the preceding [unconditioned] solely by means of the two characters "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).

By reflecting back upon this, one immediately attains it. Whenever one brings sentient beings to extinction (nirvāṇa), one does not abide in giving. To maintain recitation with faith is the foremost patience. There is no self and no dharmas;

all wholesome dharmas arise from the mind and constitute patience. Knowledge, vision, faith, and understanding are all [patience], but to abide in even a single mark is to be contrary to it. Do this to the utmost.

Amidst manifold activities, it is precisely by not dwelling on appearances that one acts in accordance with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is the appearance of the signless (*animitta*). The six things—dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning—are all empty appearances.

Yet, none of them are an emptiness devoid of substance; rather, they all enter into emptiness from within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). For example, a dream does not arise without a stimulus, and an illusion does not manifest without a technique.

Without water, bubbles do not arise; without a substance, reflections do not appear; without atmospheric conditions, dew does not descend; without terrestrial vapors, lightning does not ascend. All these emerge from existence and enter into non-existence.

From the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these two meanings are established together; they constitute the entire reality of the Buddha-dharma. Thus, the verse says: "Neither conditioned nor separate.

Although it says "not conditioned," it does not mean that it is separate from the conditioned. It further says: "The nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas [is attained] through the nine kinds of conditioned phenomena by means of sublime wisdom and correct contemplation.

This means that the dharma of the primordial nirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas is all obtained from within these nine kinds of conditioned phenomena through sublime wisdom and correct contemplation. Sublime wisdom and correct contemplation are precisely...

One perceives the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and thereby attains the true, eternal, and real mark (*bhūtatathatā*). Furthermore, the eight lines of Maitreya’s verse concerning "seeing," "marks," and "consciousness" provide a general explanation of the meaning of the ancient verses to conclude the central theme of the entire scripture.
Regarding "seeing" and "marks": all marks whatsoever; regarding "consciousness": the discrimination of marks. The "body" refers to the physical substance of the environment and the individual body;

it speaks of discriminating the existence of marks, namely these nine kinds of marks. All of these are matters of physical form and sensory experience, and are not the true mark. If one can understand this...

This is precisely right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Taking this method of right contemplation and applying it to the three periods of time, one sees that all are like these nine kinds of non-true characteristics.

Thus, within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one attains the true characteristic of unconditioned mastery, which is what is called the "stainless dharma" (*vimala-dharma*). "Stainless" means pure and signless (*animitta*).
These eight phrases truly summarize the meaning of the single dharma throughout the three periods of time as presented in the entire sutra.

The above constitutes the seventh chapter of this sutra, in which it is stated that the Buddha has neither the mark of phenomena nor the mark of non-phenomena. It then cites an ancient verse to conclude the discourse, through which the true Dharma of the Tathāgata is revealed.

According to my humble analysis, the seven sections beginning with "The Dharma-body has no marks" clearly present both the Tathāgata and the Buddha side by side, thereby revealing the meaning of their essential unity.

Therefore, I have divided this into two chapters to demonstrate that the Buddha and the Tathāgata both converge upon the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). The four-line verse is the very essence of the non-characteristic of all marks;
one who is able to contemplate in this manner sees the Tathāgata. From beginning to end, they correspond: such is the true principle, and such is the meaning of the text.

The old commentators mistakenly take the three characters "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as a refutation, annotating that within the realm of sentient beings, all conditioned activity and flux is resolved by the single character "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), thereby failing to perceive the fullness of the Buddha-dharma.

Because [the translators] did not understand the subtlety of this verse, they failed to recognize that the word *dharma* (法) is explicitly present in the original text. Furthermore, Maitreya’s verses add the words "middle" (*madhya*) and "attained" (*prāpta*). How could this not be self-evident?
In Paramārtha’s translation, following the phrase "unmoving as suchness" (*tathatā-aniñjya*), it says: "There is always the correct teaching:

one should contemplate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as being like darkness, cataracts, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud. Is this so-called "always the correct teaching" not indeed the established doctrine transmitted from antiquity? One should contemplate conditioned phenomena...

"Dharmas"—does this not indeed refer to all the dharmas throughout the entire sutra? This is what I mean when I say that this one volume of the Golden Sutra expounds nothing other than the essential purport of this verse;
I do not dare to speak thus from mere conjecture.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and all the worlds of gods and humans, [rejoiced].
The asuras, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.

This section on the circulation [of the teaching] was also established by Dao’an. As for upāsakas and upāsikās—meaning lay men and women who are able to reverently serve the Triple Gem and uphold the five precepts:

first, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from taking what is not given; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct; fourth, abstaining from false speech; and fifth, abstaining from drinking intoxicants—these are called the upāsaka precepts.
